questions.stem: A hash table finds the slot of a key by computing:
options: a binary search over the slots
questions.explanation: hash turns the key into an integer; % capacity folds it into 0..capacity - 1. (a) only works for integer keys and puts all small keys in slot 0; (c) is searching, which is what hashing avoids.

questions.stem: In a table of capacity 8, the index of the key 45 is:
The one rule every hash function must obey is:
options: the hash is a prime number
the hash is smaller than the capacity
questions.explanation: Otherwise two equal keys look in different buckets, and a key that is present is reported missing. (a) is impossible — there are more keys than hash values — and not needed: collisions are handled.

questions.stem: python -c "print(hash('abc'))" prints a different number each time you run it because:
options: it is a bug in Python
the hash of a string is its address in memory
the capacity of the table changed
string hashing uses a random secret key chosen at start-up, on purpose
questions.explanation: Hash randomisation, on by default since Python 3.3, so that an attacker cannot predict which strings collide. Within one run the hash never changes. (b) is how objects without a __hash__ of their own are hashed, not strings.

questions.stem: Which of these is the same in every run of Python?
options: the order in which a set of strings is printed
questions.explanation: hash(n) is n for every integer of this size. str and bytes hashes are randomised (b, c), and a set's order follows the hashes (d).

questions.stem: m.put([1, 2], "x") raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' because:
options: a list can change after it is stored, and then it would be in the wrong bucket
lists are too long to hash
questions.explanation: A mutable key could change after put; its hash would change with it, and it would sit in a bucket no lookup visits. So Python refuses to hash lists, dicts and sets at all.

questions.stem: 23 keys are placed in 365 slots at random. The probability that at least two share a slot is about:
questions.explanation: 1 - 365/365·364/365⋯343/365 ≈ 0.507 — the birthday paradox. 23/365 (c) is about 6% (a), the chance for one given pair, and ignores the other 252 pairs.

questions.stem: The load factor of a hash table is:
options: the number of collisions so far
the length of the longest chain
questions.explanation: For chaining it is also the average chain length.

questions.stem: A ChainingHashMap() receives put for 5, 13 and 21. Bucket 5 is:
options: 5 only; 13 and 21 are in other buckets
questions.explanation: All three are 5 mod 8, and each new key is pushed on the front: after 5, then 13 → 5, then 21 → 13 → 5. Load 3/8: no resize.

questions.stem: In the table of W13-M09, get(29) compares 29 with how many entries before raising KeyError?
questions.explanation: 29 % 8 = 5: it compares with 21, 13 and 5, reaches the end of the chain, and raises KeyError.

questions.stem: A ChainingHashMap() receives distinct keys one at a time. The first resize happens during the put of the:
questions.explanation: The check runs after the insert, with >: 6/8 = 0.75 is allowed, 7/8 = 0.875 is not. The table goes from 8 to 16 buckets during the 7th put.

questions.stem: _resize cannot copy old[i] into new[i] because:
options: the index depends on the capacity, so keys would sit where get no longer looks
the chains would come out reversed
the load factor would be wrong
questions.explanation: A key in bucket 2 of 8 (say 10) belongs in bucket 10 of 16. Copied across, it stays in bucket 2, and get(10) looks in bucket 10: KeyError. Every key must be rehashed.

questions.stem: An OpenAddressingHashMap() receives put for 6, 14 and 22. Key 22 is in slot:
options: it is not stored: slot 6 is taken
questions.explanation: 6 → slot 6. 14 → 6 is taken, slot 7. 22 → 6, 7 taken, wrap to slot 0. Slots: 22 _ _ _ _ _ 6 14.

questions.stem: In the table of W13-M13, get(30, None) makes how many probes?
questions.explanation: 30 % 8 = 6: probes 6 (6), 7 (14), 0 (22), 1 (None) — four probes, then "not there".

questions.stem: In open addressing, delete leaves a tombstone instead of None because:
options: None would cut the probe sequences that pass through the slot, and keys beyond it would become unreachable
questions.explanation: A search stops at None, because put would have used that slot. Emptying a slot in the middle of a probe sequence makes every key beyond it unreachable (test_open_addressing_delete_preserves_probe_chain).

questions.stem: get meets a tombstone while probing. It:
options: stops: the key is not in the table
questions.explanation: A tombstone means "a key was here once, and others may have probed past it". Only None ends a search.

questions.stem: put counts tombstones in its load check because:
options: otherwise tombstones can take every None, and a probe that stops only at None scans the whole table — or never stops
questions.explanation: Tombstones are not keys (a, c), but they are not None either. Uncounted, a table under many puts and deletes fills with tombstones: every miss probes the whole table, and a loop that waits for None never ends.

questions.stem: Primary clustering is:
options: chains growing long in a chaining table
runs of occupied slots in linear probing, which grow faster the longer they are
questions.explanation: A run of length L is hit by any key whose home is in it or next to it, and the key lands at its end, making it longer. (b) is not clustering in the linear-probing sense.

questions.stem: For linear probing with a good hash, Knuth's formula for an unsuccessful search is 1/2(1 + 1/(1-α)2). At α = 0.5 it gives:
questions.explanation: 1/2(1 + 1/0.25) = 1/2 · 5 = 2.5. (a) is the successful search at 0.5; (d) the unsuccessful one at 0.9. Measured in Lecture 13 on 16,384 slots: 2.56.

questions.stem: The keys 0, 1024, 2048, 3072, … (n of them) are put into a ChainingHashMap, whose capacity is always a power of two. While the capacity is at most 1,024, one get costs:
options: O(n) — every key is in bucket 0
questions.explanation: Each key is a multiple of 1,024, so key % capacity is 0 for every power-of-two capacity up to 1,024. Resizing does not help (a): the keys collide at every such capacity. One chain of n entries: O(n) per get, O(n2) to build.

questions.stem: Python's dict is:
options: open addressing, with a probe sequence that mixes in the high bits of the hash; it grows at about two-thirds full
chaining, with a linked list in every bucket
questions.explanation: CPython's Objects/dictobject.c: open addressing, probe i = (5*i + 1 + perturb) % 2**k with perturb taken from the hash, a resize at about two-thirds, and "dummy" entries as tombstones. (b) is Java's HashMap.

questions.stem: Which question does a sorted array answer in O(log n) but a hash table cannot answer faster than O(n)?
options: what is the value stored for key k?
how many keys lie between a and b?
questions.explanation: A range query needs order, and hashing destroys order on purpose: 2027114 and 2027115 land far apart. A sorted array answers it with two lower_bounds (Week 8). (a)–(c) are O(1) average in a hash table.

essays.stem: Explain how a hash table finds a key in O(1) time on average. State the assumption behind "on average", give the worst case, and name three things that can push a real table towards it.
essays.answer:
• Mechanism: the index hash(key) % capacity is computed in O(1) and the Array slot is reached in O(1); only the keys that share that slot are compared — a chain, or a short run of probes.
  • Assumption: the hash spreads the keys evenly, as if at random, and the load factor α is kept below a constant by resizing. Then a chain averages α entries (a probe run: a few slots), so get, put and delete are O(1) expected, and put amortised because of resizes.
  • Worst case: all n keys in one bucket or one cluster: O(n) per operation.
  • What pushes towards it (any three): a poor hash (sum of characters — anagrams collide); keys sharing their low bits on a power-of-two table (multiples of 1,024); an adversary who can predict the hash (hashDoS — hence string hash randomisation); no resizing, so α grows with n; open addressing near α = 1, or clogged with tombstones.

essays.stem: A student's class defines __hash__ to return 0 for every object. Is a hash table of these objects wrong, or only slow? Answer for chaining and for open addressing, and give the cost of get and of building a table of n keys.
essays.answer:
• Only slow — never wrong. Every key hashes to 0 and lands in bucket (or home slot) 0; keys are still told apart by ==, so every get finds the right entry or correctly reports it missing.
  • Chaining: one chain holding all n keys. get walks it: O(n). Each put walks it too (to check for the key): building n keys is 1 + 2 + … + n = O(n2). Resizing never helps: 0 % capacity is always 0.
  • Open addressing: all keys form one cluster starting at slot 0; a get probes up to n slots, O(n); building is O(n2) — the same.
  • The only hash rule for correctness is "equal keys, equal hashes", and a constant keeps it. Every other quality of a hash function is about speed.

essays.stem: Compare chaining and open addressing: what a slot holds, the load factors each can tolerate, how each deletes, and one practical advantage of each.
essays.answer:
• A slot holds: chaining — None or the head of a linked list of Entry nodes; open addressing — one key (in _keys) and its value (in _values), or None, or a tombstone.
  • Load factor: chaining still works above 1 (chains simply grow; cost about 1 + α), and resizes at 0.75 here; open addressing cannot exceed 1 at all and degrades sharply near it (a miss ≈ 1/2(1 + 1/(1-α)2)), so it resizes earlier — 0.66 here, about 2/3 in CPython.
  • Delete: chaining unlinks a node (the head is the special case); open addressing must leave a tombstone, which later puts may reuse and a resize drops.
  • Advantages: chaining — simple deletion, graceful at high load, never "full"; open addressing — no node per key (less memory, no allocation), and consecutive probes are neighbours in memory, which suits the cache. CPython's dict and set use open addressing; Java's HashMap uses chaining.

essays.stem: Explain tombstones. Why can an open-addressing delete not simply empty the slot? State how get, put and _resize each treat a tombstone, and why the load check must count them.
essays.answer:
• Why not empty the slot: a search stops at None. If keys a and b collide and b was placed beyond a, emptying a's slot cuts b's probe sequence: get(b) stops at the new None and reports b missing although it is still in the table.
  • get / delete: skip a tombstone and keep probing; stop only at the key or at None.
  • put: remember the first tombstone passed, but keep probing to None — the key may be further on (then overwrite it). If it is not there, insert at the remembered tombstone (reusing the space), else at the None.
  • _resize: re-insert only live keys; tombstones are dropped, so the new table has none.
  • Load check: tombstones are not keys, but they fill slots, and only None stops a probe. Counting them (size + tombstones + 1) forces a rebuild — at the same capacity if the live keys alone are within the limit — before the table runs out of None.

essays.stem: Show that a hash table that doubles its capacity when the load factor passes a fixed limit does amortised O(1) work per put on rehashing. What happens if it grows by a fixed 8 slots instead?
essays.answer:
• A resize at size s rehashes s keys. With doubling, the resizes before reaching size n happened at sizes of at most n, n/2, n/4, …, so the total rehashing is at most n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n: O(n) for n puts, amortised O(1) each. (Measured in Lecture 13: 3,075 keys rehashed for 3,000 puts in the chaining table, 5,396 in the open-addressing one — both under 2n.)
  • Growing by 8 slots: a resize every 6 or so puts, each rehashing all keys so far: 6 + 12 + 18 + … ≈ n2/12 — Θ(n2) in total, Θ(n) amortised per put. The same argument as the DynamicArray with a constant growth step (Lecture 04).
